Describe the mission and vision for the Center or Institute.
The University of Rhode Island’s Digital Forensics and Cyber Security Center (DFCSC) delivers URI’s academic programs in Digital Forensics and Cybersecurity, which include undergraduate minors, graduate certificates, and a masters degree in those fields.
The DFCSC coordinates Digital Forensics and Cybersecurity academic programs and courses with other related programs on campus including those in Criminal Justice within the College of Arts and Sciences (A&S).
DFCSC programs have been recognized by the National Security Agency (NSA) as being a national Center of Academic Excellence (CAE) in Cyber Defense, the premier academic designation in the nation. 2.
Where will the Center/Institute be located physically - or will it be organized virtually?

The DFCSC is physically located in Rooms 101 and 103 Tyler Hall, Kingston; rooms that have been dedicated to the Center for over 10 years.
The DFCSC provides Digital Forensics and Cybersecurity degree programs for the university.

Describe the balance between the teaching, service, outreach, and research missions of the Center or Institute?

The DFCSC’s focus is exclusively teaching – delivering URI’s programs in Digital Forensics and Cybersecurity.
As a smaller part of its mission, the DFCSC has performed training in digital forensics and cybersecurity for organizations.
Some faculty members associated with the DFCSC do research, but those research projects are not conducted through this Center.

The DFCSC does not seek any internal funding.

The current external funding directly associated with the DFCSC is a $3.8M National Science Foundation CyberCorps Scholarship For Service five-year grant, with Victor Fay-Wolfe as the PI.
This grant provides scholarships for students doing URI’s Professional Science Master’s Degree in Cybersecurity (which is run in the DFCSC).
The DFCSC performs self-assessment in accordance with the guidelines set forth by the NSA CAE designation.
A copy of the goals and assessment plan is attached.
Other goals include graduating at least 30 minors per year from the undergraduate programs and at least 25 students per year from its graduate programs. 5.

Which ones?

The DFCSC is a subsidiary of the URI Computer Science and Statistics Department (CS&S) and thus reports to the Chair of CS&S, and to the Dean of the College of Arts and Sciences (A&S).

The DFCSC coordinates all Digital Forensics and Cybersecurity education at URI including interdisciplinary arrangements with Criminal Justice within A&S, and coordination with other programs in Business and Engineering that involve digital forensics and/or cybersecurity.
The DFCSC has already achieved national recognition with its designation as a NSA CAE, being a recipient of the NSF CyberCorps grant, and its long-time acknowledgment as a national leader in Digital Forensics and Cybersecurity education.

There are over 100 similar Centers at other universities because the NSA CAE designation, which is the most prominent designation for Cybersecurity academic programs in the nation, requires a dedicated Center for Cybersecurity education at the institution.

URI maintaining the DFCSC as its designated Center is crucial in keeping this essential CAE designation.
Without the CAE designation, URI would lose the NSF grant and would not be able to compete in the rapidly growing Cybersecurity education field, one in which URI has been a national leader for almost 20 years.
Please see the attached 2021 support letter from the Provost stating the university’s support for the DFCSC as a Center dedicated to Cybersecurity education. 9.

The DFCSC is self-sustaining on the internal revenue generated from its academic programs.

The DFCSC was originally formed in 2004 from an NSF CyberCorps capacity building grant, with no internal URI resources.

A&S provided support from 2012-2018 for 25% FTE for the DFCSC Director position, but no longer provides that support.
